readerTitle: The fair budget that hurt every store
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 소매 체인, 레스토랑 그룹) + 실제 기업 (Yahoo 2006년 내부 메모)
insight: 여러 사업을 가진 회사는 사업마다 맡은 역할(현금 창출, 성장, 실험)이 다르므로, 같은 규칙이 아니라 역할에 맞는 기준으로 자원을 나누고 평가해야 한다.
misconception: 모든 사업부에 예산을 똑같이 나누고 같은 수익 목표를 주는 것이 공정하고 안전하다.

sources.text: Garlinghouse, B. (2006). Internal Yahoo memo ("Peanut Butter Manifesto"), published by The Wall Street Journal, November 2006.
Boston Consulting Group, the growth-share matrix (Henderson, 1970): 사업부를 성장률과 시장 점유율로 분류하는 초기 포트폴리오 도구
소매 체인과 레스토랑 그룹 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Yahoo 메모: 2006년 11월 수석 부사장 Brad Garlinghouse가 작성하고 WSJ가 공개했습니다. 회사가 투자를 땅콩버터처럼 얇게 펴 발라 아무것에도 집중하지 못한다는 내용입니다. 카드에서는 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다. 메모와 이후 Yahoo 실적 사이의 인과관계는 주장하지 않았습니다.
포트폴리오 도구가 1970년대 컨설팅 회사(BCG)를 통해 널리 퍼졌다는 서술을 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드에는 회사 이름이나 프레임워크 이름을 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The fair budget that hurt every store
body: A family runs three businesses: two old home-goods stores, a new online delivery service and a small pop-up shop.
Every year, each one gets the same budget increase. No favorites, no arguments. Three years later, all three are worse off than they should be.

image.label: Three different shops each handed an identical stack of coins
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 성격이 다른 가게 세 곳(오래된 매장, 배달 밴, 작은 팝업 부스) 앞에 똑같은 높이의 동전 더미가 하나씩 놓여 있음. 매장 앞 동전은 쓰이지 않고 쌓여 있고, 배달 밴 앞 동전은 모자라 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: You have $300,000 to invest.
body: Your old stores earn steady cash but aren't growing. Delivery is growing fast but still loses money. The pop-up is an untested idea.
How do you split the money?

options.text: $100,000 each, so every business gets a fair shot
options.feedback: It avoids arguments, but it ignores what each business needs. The stores may not use it well, and delivery gets too little to win.

options.text: Mostly to the stores, since they earn the profit
options.feedback: This rewards past results and feels safe. But it pours money into the part with the least room to grow.

options.text: Enough to keep the stores healthy, most to delivery, a small test budget for the pop-up
options.feedback: Each business gets money matched to its job. The trade-off: you must explain to store managers why they get less.

cards.title: Equal money, unequal needs.
body: The stores spent their extra money on small refits that customers barely noticed. Their market wasn't growing, so more money didn't bring more sales.
Delivery needed vans and drivers to keep up with demand. Short of money, it grew slowly while a rival grabbed the neighborhood.
The pop-up got far more than a test needed, so it kept running long after the idea had clearly failed.

cards.title: Portfolio thinking
body: **Portfolio thinking** means looking at all your businesses as one set, where each has a different job.
Some earn steady cash. Some are meant to grow. Some are cheap bets to learn if an idea works. You fund and judge each one **by its job**, not by one rule for all.
The question changes from "Is this business good?" to "What is this business for, and is it doing that?"

image.label: Three boxes labeled Earn cash, Grow, Test, with money flowing between them
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 세 개의 상자: "Earn cash", "Grow", "Test". "Earn cash" 상자에서 나온 화살표가 굵게 "Grow"로, 가늘게 "Test"로 흘러감. 각 상자 아래에 다른 측정 기준("Profit", "Customers won", "What we learned") 라벨.

cards.title: Yahoo's "peanut butter" memo
body: In 2006, a senior Yahoo executive wrote an internal memo, later published by The Wall Street Journal. He warned that the company spread its investment like peanut butter: a thin layer over everything.
His point was that funding every project a little meant no project got enough to win. He called for clearer choices about what mattered most.
Even large, well-funded companies fall into equal spreading, because it feels fair and avoids hard conversations.

image.label: A thin layer of peanut butter spread across many slices of bread
image.brief: 식빵 여러 장 위에 땅콩버터가 아주 얇게 펴 발려 있고, 한 장만 두껍게 발린 대비 이미지. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You don't need many companies to use it.
body: The same thinking works for menu items, store locations, product lines or a team's projects.
A bakery's bread may be the cash earner, a new cake line the growth bet, and a weekend market stall the test. Each deserves a different budget and a different scorecard.
Ask of every part: is it here to earn, to grow or to learn?

cards.title: Labels can become self-fulfilling.
body: Call a business a "cash earner" and starve it, and it may decline faster than it had to. Steady businesses still need upkeep.
The parts also affect each other. A low-profit item may bring in customers who buy everything else, so judge the set, not just each line.
And roles change. Review them every year, or yesterday's growth bet becomes a money pit no one questions.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant group.
body: You own a busy steakhouse that earns well and a new fast-casual spot that lost money this year but is gaining regulars. Your partner wants both to hit the same 10% profit target next year.
What do you propose?

options.text: Agree: one target for everyone keeps things simple
options.feedback: Simple, but it forces the new spot to cut staff and marketing just as it's gaining customers. You may kill your growth bet to make it look tidy.

options.text: Profit targets for the steakhouse; growth targets and a deadline for the new spot
options.feedback: Each place is judged on its job, such as repeat visits and weekly covers for the new one. The deadline stops the bet from running forever.

options.text: No targets for the new spot until it finds its feet
options.feedback: It protects the bet, but without any measure you won't know when to push harder or stop.

cards.title: Give each business a job, then fund it for that job.
body: Equal treatment feels fair but often serves no one. Decide which parts earn, which grow and which test, and judge each by its own scorecard.
**Try it today:** list your products, locations or projects. Label each one Earn, Grow or Test. Then check whether your spending matches the labels.
